title: Bound and reap notification sound workers and helper process trees
description:
## Finding

The notification-sound subsystem calls external audio and legacy shell commands synchronously on its sole bounded worker without any lifecycle deadline or process-tree containment. One hung command permanently consumes the worker, prevents every later sound and fallback from running, and can leave descendant processes behind. The documentation calls the worker bounded, but only its request queue is bounded.

### Evidence at audited commit

* `crates/thegn-host/src/notification_sound.rs:144-184` owns one long-lived worker that processes playback requests serially. The worker invokes the selected provider or legacy command inline; there is no per-request deadline, cancellation token, tree handle, or reaper.
* `crates/thegn-host/src/notification_sound.rs:298-312` implements legacy command mode as `sh -c <user configuration>` followed by blocking `.status()`. A shell or descendant can run forever, and the next queued request is never observed.
* `crates/thegn-host/src/platform/sound.rs:113-124` invokes platform helpers such as `afplay`, `pw-play`, `paplay`, `aplay`, `ffplay`, `play`, or PowerShell with the same unbounded blocking status call and only direct-child ownership.
* `crates/thegn-host/src/notification_sound.rs:78-104` also creates an unowned snapshot rebuild thread on each reload. Generation checks prevent stale installation, but repeated reloads can leave arbitrarily many concurrent filesystem/provider scans.
* `docs/help/notifications.md:131-137` says playback is on a bounded worker and overload degrades to terminal bell. The channel can reject excess work, but a hung accepted request means the worker never reaches the fallback path.

### Adversarial scenario

Configure command mode with a program that forks a descendant and waits forever, or place a hanging audio executable earlier on `PATH`. The sole worker blocks permanently. Subsequent notification sounds accumulate until the queue fills; later requests fall back to BEL, while the original shell/process tree survives reload and shutdown. Repeated configuration reloads can separately accumulate snapshot threads.

## Required design

1. Run every external sound helper and legacy command through a total-lifecycle bounded subprocess primitive with fixed stdout/stderr policy, process-group/job containment, deadline, cancellation, and verified reap.
2. Keep at most one playback active and make overload behavior explicit: coalesce or reject pending requests while guaranteeing fallback/outcome delivery does not depend on the wedged helper returning.
3. Preserve legacy shell semantics only as an explicit compatibility mode; document the trust boundary and never interpolate sound paths or notification data into shell text.
4. Own the worker and active process tree from the host lifecycle so reload/shutdown cancels and reaps promptly.
5. Coalesce reload snapshot builds to at most one active generation plus one latest requested generation.
6. Expose typed timeout/oversize/spawn/exit/reap outcomes to diagnostics instead of log-only failure.
7. Add deterministic fake-helper tests for never-exit, grandchild survival, early parent exit, repeated notifications under a hang, queue overload, reload storms, shutdown cancellation, and Windows job assignment failure.

## Acceptance criteria

* Every playback attempt has one documented wall-clock bound that includes spawn, execution, cancellation, and reap.
* No helper, descendant, zombie, pipe reader, or snapshot worker survives cancellation or host shutdown.
* One hung playback cannot suppress all future fallback/outcome reporting or grow pending memory.
* Repeated reloads keep snapshot work constant-bounded and only the newest generation may publish.
* Documentation accurately distinguishes bounded queue capacity from bounded subprocess execution.
* Linux/macOS/Windows compilation and fake-helper lifecycle tests pass.
